summary: Junior Astronaut Academy is a 3D mission trainer for kids aged 7–12. Players start on a school campus, follow glowing arrows to a rocket and choose a mission to the Moon or Mars. After a launch and landing, they live through a 4-day mission. Each day they complete hands-on science tasks as mini-games (drilling for ice, filling oxygen tanks, reading a Geiger counter), face a dilemma whose consequences appear on later days, and protect three resources: Power, Life support and Health. Day 3 brings a real hazard: a solar particle storm on the Moon, taken from real NASA DONKI events, or a dust storm on Mars. Every fact, storm and health finding comes from NASA data or published measurements and is credited in the game. This matters because it turns abstract space science into felt experience. Kids learn that real missions are about trade-offs, that every choice has a cost, and that failure is something astronauts learn from.
details:
What it does and how it works

  • Campus: a welcome tutorial explains the game, and glowing arrows lead to the rocket. A laptop there lets the player choose the Moon or Mars.
    • a day banner;
    • up to 3 tasks. There are 24 tasks in total (12 per world), using 17 different mini-games: aim solar panels at the moving Sun, steer a rover around rocks, patch spacesuit leaks, focus a microscope, keep a moonquake sensor level, photograph Mars’s blue sunset, and more.
    • a dilemma with delayed consequences, for example rover or backup battery, exercise or more science, shelter from radiation or finish the moonwalk.
  • Feedback: health loss plays a sound and makes the health bar glow red. Tasks locked by an earlier wrong decision show an alarming warning. Quizzes reward correct answers.
  • Final report: stars for Science, Health and Life support, a Gold, Silver or Bronze badge, a mission log, and a “NASA data used” screen. Then the player returns to campus to try again or try the other world.

Benefits and intended impact
Kids learn real constraints, not invented numbers: limited power, air and radiation, the effects of low gravity on bones and muscles, and Earth–Mars communication delays. Because there are two worlds, random real storms and a star rating, they replay the game and learn from failure without being punished. Teachers can use it in class to start discussions about mission planning and space science.

Creativity

  • Real data drives the story: real 2024 solar storms are the in-game hazard.
  • Every task is its own mini-game, so kids do the science instead of reading about it.
  • Consequences arrive later, the way they do in real mission planning.
  • Each world has its own look and sound: a silver Moon theme, a rust Mars theme, dust storms, a siren and a Geiger counter, all with sound generated in code.

What we considered

  • Age group: plain language for ages 7–12, with terms like sol, regolith and mSv explained in context.
  • Simplicity: only three core resources.
  • No free choices: every option in a dilemma has a cost.
  • Honest data: archived data is never presented as live.
  • Accessibility: text size, mouse sensitivity, invert Y, field of view, volume, graphics and resolution settings, plus a pause menu and big, clear buttons.
  • Performance: a lighter-model tool for the very heavy 3D models, background loading of the next scene, and pre-rendered cinematics.


    Tools and languages
    Unity 6 (Universal Render Pipeline), C#, TextMeshPro, Unity Recorder, glTFast, Blender (asset inspection), Windows desktop build. Claude (Anthropic) was used as an AI coding assistant.
